tip: Nous faisons is pronounced 'fuh-zon,' not 'fay-zon' – only in forms of faire does that ai go to a silent schwa. Nous faisons une promenade.
'Viens de Lyon' means come FROM Lyon – an origin. But venir de + a verb means 'just did': je viens de manger = I just ate. The next word decides.
For food and drink, prendre (to take) means 'to have': tu prends un croissant = you're having a croissant, not grabbing one to go.
Mettre means 'to put,' so tu mets la table is literally 'you put the table' – French's way of saying 'you set the table.'
English 'leave' splits in French: sortir is going out for the evening ('sors ce soir'); quitter is leaving a place or person behind.
Body features take the definite article, not 'some': 'a les yeux bleus' is literally 'has THE blue eyes', never des yeux bleus.
Du café means 'some coffee' – du (de + le) is the 'some' French won't drop even where English omits it: qui veut du café ?
French doesn't say your back hurts – you 'have pain at' it: tu as mal au dos, literally 'you have evil at the back.' Pattern: avoir mal à + body part.
'Où se trouve...?' = Where is...located? More formal than 'Où est...?' Both are correct.

target: Bonne nuit, faites de beaux rêves!
tip: When an adjective comes before a plural noun, des shrinks to de: not des beaux rêves but de beaux rêves. Faites de beaux rêves!

target: Est-ce que vous avez une chambre ?
tip: 'Est-ce que' is the easiest way to form questions – just add it before a statement. No word order change needed.
Age is something you HAVE in French: 'j'ai vingt-cinq ans' is literally 'I have twenty-five years'. Être here would be wrong.
'À le' is never said in French – it must contract to au: 'vais au cinéma', not à le cinéma.
'À l'aéroport' uses the contracted 'à l'' before vowels. Full form would be 'à le', but that doesn't exist.
Belle comes before its noun: 'une belle maison', not maison belle. A few short common adjectives (beau, grand, petit) lead like this.
'Je suis' is both 'I am' (être) and 'I follow' (suivre). Here it's following: 'je suis la leçon' = I follow the lesson, not I am it.
'Chez' means 'to/at the place of'. Use with people: chez le médecin, chez moi (at my place), chez Paul.

english: An hour is enough for me.
tip: Il me suffit works impersonally: 'il me suffit d'une heure' is literally 'it suffices me an hour' = an hour is enough for me. The amount you need takes de.

english: We have been friends for a long time.
tip: French stays in the present with depuis: nous sommes amis depuis longtemps is literally 'we are friends since long' for 'we have been friends.'

english: They have a lot of patience.
tip: 'Beaucoup de' (much/many) is always followed by 'de', never 'des': beaucoup de patience, beaucoup d'amis.

target: Ils ont soif après le match.
english: They are thirsty after the game.
tip: Sensations are things you HAVE in French: 'ont soif' = have thirst, not 'are thirsty'. Cold and fear too: avoir froid, avoir peur.

target: Nous avons faim après la randonnée.
english: We are hungry after the hike.
tip: 'Nous avons faim' is literally 'we have hunger'. Watch out – 'je suis faim' would mean you ARE hunger itself.

english: Do you have a menu in English?
tip: Flipping verb and subject makes a formal question: 'Avez-vous un menu' = do you have a menu. Casual speech just says vous avez un menu ?

target: Elle sort du bureau à cinq heures.
english: She leaves the office at five.
tip: Du is de + le fused: 'sort du bureau' = leaves the office, literally 'out OF the office'. De le is never said.
'Avoir tort' = to be wrong, 'avoir raison' = to be right. French 'has wrong/reason'.
You HAVE dizziness in French, you don't feel it: j'ai le vertige = "I have the vertigo". Note the le – a definite article where English uses none.
Nationalities aren't capitalized in French when used as adjectives: vous êtes français, not Français.
'Être d'accord' = to agree. Literally 'to be of agreement'. Very common expression.
French is "in anger", not "angry": il est en colère. Lots of states take en this way, like être en retard (late).
'Avoir confiance en' = to trust / to have confidence in. Another avoir expression for a feeling.
